name: NIST Assembly Task Boards
ability_definition: The ability to make precisely coordinated movements of the fingers of one or both hands to grasp, manipulate, or assemble very small objects.

task_realism.reasoning: The tasks closely match real small-part assembly work in electronics, mechanical and wire-harness manufacturing. They include threading nuts and screws, inserting pegs, seating electrical connectors, meshing gears, routing belts and wiring, and snap fits. The part sizes and operations reflect genuine factory kitting and assembly. Two gaps keep it below the top: the parts are mostly standard industrial parts rather than the very small items typical of watchmaking, micro-electronics rework or surgical work, and the board is a curated sampler rather than a real product.

evaluation_conditions.reasoning: Testing happens in a controlled lab, and the board layout is known in advance. CAD data, custom fixtures and tools are allowed, and parts are often pre-positioned in kits. Real work involves variable part presentation, tolerance variation, clutter, and sustained throughput and quality demands over long shifts. Those conditions are largely absent. The time limit and time bonus add some realistic time pressure. Because the board changes every edition, conditions are not stable across years, and the end-effector setup behind top scores is unverified.

construct_coverage.reasoning: The O*NET ability concerns precisely coordinated finger movements used to grasp and manipulate very small objects. The benchmark is hardware-agnostic, so parallel grippers, specialized tools and fixtures can succeed without anything resembling coordinated multi-finger dexterity. It scores task outcome, not coordination or in-hand manipulation. Deformable and fine-scale items, tactile-driven adjustment, and bimanual fine coordination are only partially sampled. It captures the 'assemble small objects' slice well but under-covers the finger-coordination core.

format_match.reasoning: Inputs are real physical components and outputs are physically completed assemblies checked against objective success criteria, which resemble real assembly QA outcomes. The format is not an abstraction. Two things make it artificial: the scoring is point-based with time bonuses rather than yield or defect rates, and the product is a test board rather than a functional device.

transferability_reasoning: The NIST task boards use real physical small-part assembly operations with objective outcome scoring, so task realism and format match are strong. Transfer to Finger Dexterity specifically is limited because the benchmark permits grippers, fixtures, tools and CAD pre-knowledge in a controlled lab, and it scores task completion rather than coordinated finger manipulation. Success is therefore meaningful evidence of structured industrial assembly capability, but only moderate evidence of human-like fine finger dexterity in variable real-world settings.

2023.model_or_system: Team SDU robotic assembly system (RGMC IROS 2020 Manufacturing Track)
2023.metric: competition points (273 possible task points plus a time bonus; 92 for disassembly and 181 for assembly)
2023.human_reference: Specialist workforce: electromechanical and electronic assemblers and similar manual small-parts assembly workers
